## Model

|  |  |
|---|---|
| Registered model | `dnabarcode-router` |
| Version | 5 (alias `@candidate`) |
| Task | Predict the broad group (for animals, the order) of a COI barcode |
| Input | A DNA sequence (A, C, G, T; ambiguous bases allowed) |
| Output | One of 455 labels, with a confidence |
| Model | Logistic regression on 8-mer frequencies, rescaled to unit length, alpha 1e-07 |
| Calibration | Length-aware temperature, from v4 |
| Training data | MIDORI2 GB273 (CO1), [doi:10.5281/zenodo.22685701](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22685701), CC-BY-4.0 |
| Built with | prokopton-ml 0.1.0 |

## Intended use

The router is the first step of identification: it decides which broad
group (or, for animals, which order) a COI barcode most likely belongs to,
so a specialist model can identify it further. It is meant for COI sequences
of at least 100 bases; shorter sequences are declined, and
sequences under 300 bases are shown with a note that accuracy is
lower.

It is not meant for identifying species on its own, for other genes or
markers, for random stretches of a genome, for mixed samples, or for
decisions with legal, medical or regulatory consequences without expert
review.

## Data

Records were split by species: *known* species appear in training, while *novel* species are held out entirely, so their scores show how the model handles species it has never seen. Novel-species records with a near-copy (99% identity or more) in training were found with VSEARCH; *clean* records have none, and are the honest measure.

Training samples were capped at 2,000 records per class (validation: 200), spread across as many species as possible. Classes with under 20 records were left out (119 of them), and 66,593 validation records with a near-copy in training were removed.

| Sample | Records | Classes | Species per class |
|---|---|---|---|
| Training | 347,404 | 455 | 338 |
| Validation, known species | 38,222 | 455 | 58 |
| Validation, novel species | 18,971 | 334 | 18 |

## Training

In the final round of the search, 3 candidate models were compared on the validation samples (never the test sets), and the best was chosen by the mean macro-F1 across them (earlier rounds are described in the development notes). Each training record also gave 1 random fragment of 75-600 bases, so the model learns short inputs too. Every candidate is recorded in MLflow (run `e4e39c7edae04d90b726f23116c8ea47`).

| Validation set | Accuracy | Macro-F1 |
|---|---|---|
| Known species | 99.1% | 0.977 |
| Novel species | 96.7% | 0.897 |
| Known species, fragments | 94.6% | 0.916 |
| Novel species, fragments | 88.1% | 0.775 |

## Calibration

Confidence was corrected with a temperature that depends on length, T = exp(-0.2810 - 0.0091 * ln(length)), fitted on the validation samples (whole sequences and new random fragments). It changes only confidence, never the prediction. *ECE* (expected calibration error) is the average gap between confidence and accuracy; 0 is perfect.

| Validation set | Accuracy | Mean confidence | ECE |
|---|---|---|---|
| Validation, known species | 99.1% | 96.4% → 99.0% | 0.028 → 0.002 |
| Validation, known species, fragments | 94.4% | 85.7% → 93.4% | 0.086 → 0.011 |
| Validation, novel species | 96.7% | 92.3% → 96.5% | 0.044 → 0.007 |
| Validation, novel species, fragments | 87.9% | 78.7% → 88.4% | 0.092 → 0.012 |

## Test results

Measured once, on test sets the model and its selection never saw. *Accuracy* counts every record equally; *macro-F1* gives every class equal weight, so rare groups count as much as common ones.

| Test set | Records | Accuracy | Top-5 | Macro-F1 | Confidence | ECE |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Known species | 295,842 | 99.1% | 99.8% | 0.973 | 98.5% | 0.006 |
| Novel species (all) | 90,195 | 98.2% | 99.6% | 0.901 | 97.9% | 0.005 |
| Novel species (clean) | 58,592 | 97.5% | 99.4% | 0.891 | 97.3% | 0.006 |
| Novel species (leaky) | 31,603 | 99.6% | 99.9% | 0.969 | 99.1% | 0.005 |

7,311 test records had no group or order label, and 145 belonged to classes too rare to train on; these were not scored.

## Limitations

- **Short sequences** are much less accurate (at 100 bases, 65% accurate for novel species (clean)); below 100 bases they are declined.
- **Rare classes** have few reference records, so their scores vary more (see *Hardest classes*). Classes too rare to train on are never predicted.
- **The reference data reflects what has been sequenced**: GenBank holds far more records for some groups and regions than others, and some records are misidentified.
- **Only COI** sequences are supported; the marker classifier checks this first.
- **Confidence** is calibrated on validation data like the test data; on sequences unlike the reference data (contaminated, chimeric, or from a poorly sampled group) it may be too high.

## Development notes

These notes are written by hand and included in the generated card.

### How the model was chosen

The search ran in rounds, each narrowed by the last; every candidate of
every round is kept in MLflow. Scores are the mean macro-F1 on validation.

1. **Naive Bayes and logistic regression, k = 5 to 8.** Naive Bayes did best
   at the smallest smoothing tried (0.01, score 0.786). The k-mer features
   are frequencies adding up to 1 per sequence, so useful smoothing is very
   small. Logistic regression did poorly (about 0.2): its features were too
   small in scale to learn from in 15 passes.
2. **Smaller smoothing, and logistic regression on features rescaled to
   unit length.** Naive Bayes reached 0.888 (k = 8); logistic regression
   reached 0.934 (k = 6), at the smallest regularisation tried.
3. **Logistic regression at k = 8 and less regularisation.** 0.949
   (k = 8, alpha 1e-8). Gains were shrinking (+0.015, then +0.006 for the
   last step in alpha), so the search stopped.
4. **Training on random fragments.** See below. Candidates were then chosen
   on validation fragments as well as whole sequences, so this round's
   scores (the mean over four validation sets) cannot be compared with
   earlier rounds'. Logistic regression at k = 8 won again, now at
   alpha 1e-7 (0.891, against 0.888 for alpha 1e-8 and 0.857 for the best
   naive Bayes).

The ambiguity threshold for training records (0.01 to 0.10) made no real
difference in any round (about ±0.001).

### Short sequences: found on the test set

The first evaluated model (v3) scored 98.6% (known species) and 96.7%
(novel species, clean) on whole sequences, but was much less accurate on
short fragments, and overconfident: at 100 bases, 41% accurate with an
average confidence of about 62%. This was found with the test set, not the
validation set. Training on fragments fixes the method rather than tuning a
setting to the test scores, and from then on fragments were part of
validation, so model choice no longer depended on the test set; but the
test set did inform that change, which is why it is recorded here.

Training on fragments (one per record, 75-600 bases) raised accuracy at
every length, including whole sequences, but left the model underconfident
(average confidence 93.5% for 97.5% accuracy). Calibrating with a
length-aware temperature fixed that. The fitted length term was close to
zero: a single temperature (about 0.75) suits every length from 75 to 600
bases.

### Validation and test scores

For v3, macro-F1 on novel species was much lower on the test set (0.855)
than on validation (0.920). For v5 the two nearly match (0.891 against
0.897). Two differences remain worth knowing: the validation samples were
balanced (capped per class) and left out records with over 10% ambiguous
bases, while the test sets keep the natural mix, where rare classes have
few records and noisier scores; and choosing the best of many candidates
makes the validation score slightly optimistic. The test scores are the
ones to rely on.

### Future work

- Logistic regression at k = 9 (each candidate takes 30-40 minutes here).
- A small convolutional network, as a stronger comparison.
- Fitting calibration on even shorter fragments, if inputs under 100 bases
  are ever to be accepted.
